reader.summary: Singapore faced a dual squeeze from Indonesia this week. The country cut pipeline gas exports to Singapore by roughly nine percent, prompting Singapore's top envoy to travel to Jakarta to soothe what it called Indonesian angst. Simultaneously, toxic haze from Indonesian wildfires choked the city-state, forcing runners to jog in shopping malls and leading the central bank to instruct banks to monitor clients' haze-related risks. Singapore and Indonesia agreed to stand up a joint task force on illegal burning, and Singapore expanded its haze inquiries to ten locally based firms. On the economic front, third-quarter layoffs hit their highest level since 2020, while PM Wong vowed more support for workers and energy security. Singapore also announced it will store Saudi Arabian oil in underground caverns starting in 2027, plans to expand power capacity by 26 percent in the early 2030s, and granted Petronas conditional approval for a regional power corridor. The city-state explored alternatives to air conditioning as a climate measure. Keppel reported a nine-month profit jump on infrastructure demand, and Mapletree is reportedly eyeing a 2027 Singapore IPO. The WTA Singapore Open and a Brazil friendly against Japan and Singapore rounded out a lighter sports slate.

display.eli5:
Singapore has been dealing with two problems from its big neighbour Indonesia at the same time. Smoke from fires in Indonesia has made the air in Singapore really bad to breathe, so people have been running in shopping malls instead of on the streets. At the same time, Indonesia cut the amount of natural gas it sends to Singapore through underground pipes, which makes energy more expensive and uncertain.

The reason both problems are happening at once is that Indonesia is going through its own political and economic stresses, and Singapore depends heavily on its neighbour for both clean air and energy. The two countries have now agreed to set up a joint task force to figure out how to stop the illegal burning that causes the haze.

Next week, the smoke will probably get better because rain is expected in Indonesia. But the political tension will not go away. The task force will likely meet and produce a first set of rules or commitments. Singapore will also start working out the details of its new energy plans, like storing Saudi oil underground and building more power plants. And the government will probably announce something specific to help the workers who lost their jobs in the third quarter.

A surprise would be if Indonesia starts linking the haze argument to other trade issues, making the whole relationship more tense than just a smoke problem.
